evidence: Verified against cf222a0 patch: before the fix the loop did if (body.trimEnd().endsWith(REVIEW_MARKER)) count++; and then called parseCostMarker(body) unconditionally, so a body carrying a marker but not ending with the sentinel fed cost without feeding count. Not hypothetical: this PR own review bodies discuss the marker format, which F10 later proved shadows the real marker.
guidance_note: When one predicate defines a domain concept (an agent review round), route every value derived from that concept through the same predicate in the commit that adds the derivation, not just the original counter.

evidence: Same defect as F1 on a second thread; the ungated parseCostMarker call is visible in the removed lines of cf222a0. The agent posted the identical reply to both.

The silent-drop path is real - before the fix a null parse incremented neither knownRounds nor unknownRounds - but the negative-cost trigger the reviewer names is unreachable, since computeCostUsd and total_cost_usd are non-negative by construction, as the agent said. The fix routes every non-number to unknownRounds.
guidance_note: When a reviewer names one value class a pattern rejects, enumerate the whole accept-set of that pattern in the same pass - the agent fixed the rejected-value path and left the loose character class accepting a bare dot and 123..456, which cost the next round.

evidence: Third thread on the same ungated parseCostMarker call; its second clause - a markerless agent round incrementing neither counter - was also real and is what the unknownRounds branch of the fix addresses.

I ran it: Number of a bare dot and of 1.2.3 are both NaN and the old regex matches both, so the typeof cost === number gate passed and usd became NaN - real. But the 1e999 example is wrong: the regex does not match that body at all, so the Infinity path it claims is unreachable. cf222a0, the F3 fix, rewrote the loop but left COST_MARKER_RE loose, so the F3 reply claim that any value which cannot be returned as a number is counted as an unknown-cost round and never silently dropped was false when it was written.
guidance_note: A fix that claims a value class is now handled must be checked against the producer of those values - here the accept-set of the regex - not only against the consumer branch that was edited.

evidence: Same NaN-poisoning defect as F5 and it cites only real examples. Both exist because cf222a0 left the loose regex in place while claiming the unknown-round branch covered every non-number.

The asymmetry is real - the ca8882b patch adds Number.isFinite to parseCostMarker and leaves costMarker rendering cost.usd.toFixed(6) whenever cost.available. The escalation is false: I ran it and Infinity toFixed returns the string Infinity rather than throwing RangeError, so no crash was possible. The agent accepted the whole finding including the false crash claim.
guidance_note: When a fix hardens one side of a produce/parse round-trip, harden the other side in the same commit - the missing half is the next round finding.

evidence: Real gap: the pagination test 101 bodies were bare REVIEW_MARKER strings and it asserted only the count, so cost accumulation across a page boundary had no assertion. Flagged on ca8882b but not caused by it - the pagination test and its count-only assertion predate the review, and ca8882b added only marker tests.
guidance_note: When a function return widens from a scalar to a record, extend the existing tests of that function to the new fields rather than only adding tests for the new fields in isolation.

evidence: I checked the c4ec999 src/run.js patch: the core.warning and core.info lines are context lines, so the logging predates the PR exactly as the agent claimed, and the pure parts - renderCostLine, costWarning, costMarker - already live in usage.js. The law places effects AT the boundary, which run.js is, and the reviewer own text concedes the boundary is appropriately thin. Flagged on ca8882b, but the signature change came in the round-0 commit.

Real and live: body.match without the g flag returns the first occurrence while the authoritative marker trails all prose, and the reviews on this very PR quote the marker pattern in their summaries. Flagged on 8f15ff1, but the single-match read in parseCostMarker was written in c4ec999 and untouched by that commit.
guidance_note: When a machine-readable marker is embedded in text that may also discuss the marker format, read it by position - last occurrence, or adjacent to the trailing sentinel - rather than by first match.

evidence: A genuine but marginal hole: the renderPrTotal case with this-round cost available crossed with mixed known/unknown prior rounds had no direct assertion, only the two neighbouring combinations. renderPrTotal and its tests both landed in c4ec999, so the gap is original, not fix-caused.
guidance_note: A pure renderer taking two independently-varying inputs gets its cross product covered at the unit level in the commit that introduces it.

evidence: The invariant hole is real, but the crash claim is false - I ran it and NaN toFixed returns the string NaN rather than throwing RangeError, so the failure mode is a wrong render, not an opaque crash. The gap exists because 8f15ff1, the F7 fix, added Number.isFinite to costMarker alone; the f22ffcc message and patch confirm the agent instead enforced finiteness at the three construction sites, which is the better fix.
guidance_note: When adding a finiteness or shape guard for a shared value, either enforce the invariant at every construction site or guard every consumer - guarding exactly one consumer manufactures a divergence the next round will find.

evidence: The reply says fixed in f22ffcc, but I read that commit: its only test change is a computeCostUsd NaN case, and no renderPrTotal unavailable-cost unit test exists on main today. The reply is the sibling threads NaN-invariant text pasted onto a missing-test thread, so it neither answers nor fixes the finding. The gap itself is the half of renderPrTotal coverage that 9f61bd3, the F11 fix, did not add.
guidance_note: Never reuse one thread fix reply on a sibling thread that asked for something else; a missing-test finding needs a reply that names the test that was added.

evidence: The divergence is exactly the one 8f15ff1 created: costMarker guarded, renderCostLine and renderPrTotal not, so the round would print a dollar-NaN cost line while the marker the next round sums says unknown. Fixed at the sources in f22ffcc rather than by mirroring the guard, which is the correct direction under no-defensive-null-guards.

narrative: A cost-marker feature that took five rounds, and the fix chain is the reason for two of them. The four round-0 findings were three duplicates of one ungated-parse defect plus a regex complaint; the agent fixed the gate but declined to tighten the regex, and round 1 found nothing but the NaN the loose regex admits. The round-1 fix then hardened the parser and not the producer, and round 2 found the producer; the round-2 producer guard created a producer/renderer divergence, and round 4 found that. Three of the reviewer escalations were checkably false - toFixed throwing RangeError on NaN and on Infinity, and a 1e999 the regex cannot match - and the agent accepted all of them without checking. The final fixes merged with no review round at all, and one of them, the F13 test, never actually happened.
guidance_observations: Three round-0 threads (F1, F2, F4) were one finding and the agent answered each separately, which is three replies and no extra safety.

The reviewer twice asserted a RangeError crash from Number.prototype.toFixed that does not occur; a one-line node check would have downgraded both findings, and the agent replies repeated the false severity back.
The last fix commit landed and the PR merged within seconds, so f22ffcc was never reviewed - and it silently omitted one of the three things its replies claimed.

evidence: The arithmetic checks out: 0.435 over 0.003625 is 120 but 0.14 over 0.0028 is 50, so a comment stating one 120x ratio over the rates below, plural, is wrong for v4-flash. The ON-POST-REVIEW-COMMIT flag is a false positive - I read f246ec5 and it changes only the version string in package.json; the comment landed in 7276a34, the pre-review commit round 0 read and approved.
guidance_note: A comment that states a numeric ratio must be checked against every value it covers, not only the value that motivated writing it.

narrative: A seven-line docs-only PR that cost three review rounds. Round 0 read the new comment and approved it; round 1 read the same comment - the only intervening commit was a version bump - and found it misleading. The agent fix was right and minimal: drop the drift-prone multiplier and keep only the load-bearing fact. Nothing here was caused by a fix.
guidance_observations: The repo own policy that a src change must bump the version produced a package.json-only commit, which re-triggered a full review round on an unchanged diff.
The reviewer approved a comment in round 0 and faulted the identical comment in round 1 - two verdicts on one input, which is reviewer variance rather than agent churn.

evidence: ProtocolError extends Error directly and TypeError is a sibling subclass, so no value can be an instance of both; the negated conjunct can never fail and therefore asserts nothing.
guidance_note: Do not write an assertion whose failure is unrepresentable - if no value in the domain can violate it, it is decoration, not a test.

evidence: Real: writeRecords called fs.mkdtempSync per invocation and the afterEach hook removed nothing, so each test call left a directory behind. The cited law is about errors surfacing loudly; a leaked temp dir suppresses no error, so the token is decorative here even though the fix is right.
guidance_note: A test helper that creates a filesystem resource registers its teardown in the same commit that creates it.

evidence: The asymmetry - an exhausted ProtocolError reds the run while a TransientError advances the config chain - was stated only in a comment, and the produceReview tests exercised TransientError and plain Error. A refactor to isRetryableSpawnError would have flipped it with nothing failing.
guidance_note: When a comment records a deliberate asymmetry between two error types, the commit that writes the comment writes the test that pins it.

evidence: Byte-for-byte the same temp-dir leak as F2, on a second thread three lines up; the agent recognised it as a duplicate and fixed both with one change.

narrative: Four findings in round 0, all test hygiene, none a production defect; round 1 was clean. The agent accepted all four and the fixes were correct and small. Two of the four, F2 and F4, were the same temp-dir leak raised twice, so the real finding count was three.
guidance_observations: The reviewer own dedup did not collapse two threads on the same leak in the same helper three lines apart - duplicate threads are a recurring tax across this batch.

Round 0 named a genuine pre-existing gap in its summary - JSON.parse throwing a plain SyntaxError past the retry seam - but did not raise it as a finding, so the one substantive issue it saw went unrecorded.

evidence: unquoteCStylePath is a new byte-level decoder with an octal path, a nine-entry escape table and an unknown-escape fallback, exercised only through three parseUnifiedDiff integration tests. The agent noted it traced each named case and found no bug - the tests lock behavior rather than fix one.
guidance_note: A new byte-level decoder ships with direct unit tests over its escape table in the same commit; integration coverage through the caller does not pin the branches.

evidence: Checked the repo: main in package.json is dist/index.js, there is no npm publish anywhere in scripts or workflows, and the header line of src/index.js reads Re-exports for test imports. The consumer contract is action.yml plus the built dist consumed via uses, so parseUnifiedDiff has no external caller to break and the reviewer breakage premise is false.

narrative: Two round-0 findings, one accepted and one correctly declined; round 1 was clean and the PR closed in two rounds. The pushback on the breaking-public-API finding was verifiable and verified - this repo ships an Action, not a library. The accepted finding was a real coverage gap in a new byte-level decoder that the original commit should have shipped tests for.
guidance_observations: The reviewer treated every symbol in a re-export barrel as public API without checking whether the package is published - a distribution question it could have answered from package.json.
The agent pushback did the check the reviewer skipped and cited the evidence, which is what made the decline hold in one round.

evidence: I verified all three of the agent counter-claims. node --test defaults to process isolation, as node own man page shows in its config equivalence, so each test file has its own process.env; grep shows the only references to process.env.GITHUB_TOKEN in src and test are the four lines inside this one test; and the test body is fully synchronous with the restore in a finally, so there is no interleaving window even under same-process concurrency.

narrative: One round, one advisory, correctly declined, merged. The reviewer proposed a test-isolation refactor for a race that the runner default isolation, the absence of any other reader, and the test synchrony each independently rule out. The agent decline enumerated all three reasons and each of them checks out against the installed node and the repo.
guidance_observations: This is the shape of a good pushback - three independent disproofs, the weakest stated first and the airtight one last, each checkable from the machine.

evidence: Real interaction gap: dedupeFindings keeps the first-seen slot but replaces its value on a severity upgrade, so an exact-anchored advisory replaced by a snapped blocking flips both the severity and whether the survivor carries snappedFromLine. The severity upgrade and the exact-plus-snapped collapse were each tested; their combination was not.
guidance_note: When a merge keeps a first-seen slot but swaps its value on an upgrade, test the case where the swap changes a second attribute of the survivor, not only the attribute that drove the swap.

narrative: One advisory in round 0, accepted, fixed with a targeted test; round 1 clean. The finding was the interaction the change itself introduced - post-anchor dedup running the same severity-replacement the pre-anchor merge already ran - and the agent reply named the flip precisely before writing the test.
guidance_observations: The one finding was about the combination of two behaviors the PR joined, which is the kind of case a change author is best placed to enumerate before pushing - a cross product of the two states the newly-shared function is now called in.

evidence: Real: TIER_RANK indexed by an unlisted rung is undefined, Math.abs of undefined minus target is NaN, NaN is never less than bestDist, so the entry is skipped and the function can return null with no signal - while the same function throws on an unknown input tier. The union contract was stated in a comment and enforced nowhere.
guidance_note: Validate both sides of a lookup symmetrically: a function that throws on an unknown key from the caller must not silently trust the keys of the collection it is matching against.

evidence: The literals did mirror the two adapter effort arrays, but the reviewer fix - importing the live adapter arrays into a pure-algorithm test - would make a pure function expected values shift with adapter config. The agent instead made the fixture visibly synthetic and added a subset invariant over the live registry, which is where the adapter-to-ladder relationship actually belongs.
guidance_note: When a pure-algorithm fixture happens to equal a real config array, make it visibly synthetic so it cannot read as a stale copy of the config.

evidence: Same root cause as F1, argued from the maintenance scenario where an adapter gains a rung, TIER_RANK is not updated, and reasoning effort silently drops. The mechanism is the NaN comparison and it is real.
Third thread on the same asymmetric validation; it is also the one that proposed the subset-invariant test the agent adopted, so the consolidated fix came out of this thread second option.
Fourth thread on the identical NaN-skip path; the single agent reply text was posted to all four and the fix - up-front validation of engineEfforts plus a registry subset test - resolves all four.

Verified at 8761793: the only two producers of a profile are defaultEffortProfile, an object literal, and scripts/local-review.js, which parses the workers flag and throws on a non-positive integer before spreading it into the profile - so an empty effort object is unproducible, exactly as the agent said. The agent also correctly noted the failure would be a loud TypeError rather than a silent one, so the reviewer law citation misfires. Flagged on the fix commit, but the effort seam it points at was introduced in the round-0 commit 7886dd4.

narrative: Five round-0 threads that are really two findings - four restatements of one asymmetric-validation hole and one about test fixtures mirroring adapter config. The agent spotted the duplication, wrote one consolidated fix of up-front validation plus a registry subset invariant, and answered all four threads with the same text. The single round-1 finding was on the seam the original commit wrote, not on anything the fix changed, so the second round bought a fresh opinion rather than a consequence.
guidance_observations: Four of five round-0 threads were one root cause; the agent consolidated the fix correctly but still paid four replies, and the reviewer dedup did not collapse them.

The round-1 finding proposed a consumer-side guard against a state no producer can create, and the agent decline named the producing seam and the epic increment where validation actually belongs, which is the right shape for a not-yet decline.

evidence: I read CLAUDE.md at 9603b02: it defines patch as a bug fix or internal change where inputs and observable behavior are unchanged, and minor as any consumer-visible change, and the action shipped surface is action.yml plus the dist consumed via uses. The ledger module in this PR is unwired substrate adding no input, no output and no observable behavior, and the exports in src/index.js are labelled Re-exports for test imports - the package is never npm published. Generic library semver does not govern here.

narrative: One round, one advisory about the semver level, correctly declined against the repo own written versioning policy, merged. The reviewer applied library semver to a GitHub Action whose consumer contract is its YAML interface, and conceded as much inside the finding itself before recommending the change anyway.
guidance_observations: The reviewer stated the disqualifying fact - that the Action consumer-facing interface is its YAML inputs and outputs rather than these Node exports - and still recorded the finding, a self-refuting advisory that cost a thread.
The decline held because the repo documents its versioning rule in CLAUDE.md and the agent quoted it; a policy written down is what makes a one-round decline possible.

evidence: Real gap: the floor path where even the cheapest candidate exceeds the cap - the guarantee that a minimal review always runs - had coverage only at the chooseProfile unit level, never through the resolveBudgetedEffort boundary that wires the ledger read and the diff size into it.
guidance_note: A boundary helper whose whole guarantee is that a runnable value always comes back ships the failing-side case of that guarantee in the commit that introduces it.

evidence: I read README.md at 956f227: every empty-default input renders as an em dash - SCOPE, ZAI_SYSTEM_PROMPT, CONFIG, GITHUB_REVIEW_TOKEN and all four API keys - so the proposed one-row change would introduce the inconsistency it claims to remove. The literal README-versus-action.yml conflation is real but table-wide. The agent conclusion is right; the law token is not, because action.yml IS the source of truth for defaults and the README is the derived rendering, so citing one-source-of-truth to defend the rendering inverts the law.

Real and user-visible: the ledger-read failure warning said issues read while the feature post-review append needs issues write, so a user who follows the message fixes the read and fails on the append next run. Flagged on d42d689, but that commit touched only test/budget-wiring.test.js; the message was written in the original PR.
guidance_note: A diagnostic that tells the user which permission to grant names the permission the whole feature needs, not the permission the one failing call needed.

evidence: The coupling is real but the proposed cure does not cure it: resolveBudgetedEffort emits through core as part of its job, so extracting it to its own module leaves the actions-core dependency the reviewer objects to unless a logger seam is added that exists only for the test. The reviewer itself called it test noise today, not a correctness bug.

Verified the ordering in src/run.js at 726018e: prIsFromFork is at line 232 and summarizePriorReviews at 259, both already ahead of buildConfigChain at 316 and preflightChain at 322, and the billed runMultiScope spawn is at 349, behind preflight. So cheap GitHub-API gating before the provider probe is the established pattern, the diff fetch fits it, and the cost is one or two unbilled calls on a misconfigured run - which the reviewer itself calls not a new regression.

Real: the includes check passes only because defaultBudgetCandidates returns the caller object by reference, and the following lines already assert the behavior the test exists for, so the identity check adds only a refactor trap. The assertion was written in the original PR, not in the fix commit the flag names.
guidance_note: Assert membership by value when the property under test is that this candidate is offered, never by object identity, which pins the producer allocation strategy instead.

evidence: Export-for-test is real coupling, but resolveBudgetedEffort performs the ledger read and emits through core, so it cannot move into the pure budget.js, and driving it through run would require mocking the github context, core.getInput, octokit and the transport for no added safety. The exports line was added in the original PR, not by 9b39ba7. This is the F4 objection re-raised in a second form after the agent had already declined it.

A genuine user-facing bug and the best finding in this PR: a positive daily budget means the feature is on, not that the budget lowered the cap, so an ample budget produced a skip message blaming the gradient and telling the user to raise a budget that was never the constraint. The agent discriminator, comparing the resolved roundCap against the default roundCap, is the right one.
guidance_note: When a message attributes an outcome to a cause, the discriminator must test the cause itself, not the fact that the feature that could have caused it is enabled.

evidence: Real brittleness: the roundCap-below-five assertion holds only because the calibration constants make the ceiling unaffordable, so a recalibration false-fails a correct implementation. The agent chose neither of the reviewer two options and used a monotonicity sweep over descending budgets, which is calibration-independent and pins the actual shape of the gradient. Note the reply posted a literal unexpanded git rev-parse shell substitution as the fix sha; the fix is really dc43409.
guidance_note: A threshold assertion over a calibrated estimate is a calibration test in disguise - assert the shape, such as monotonicity, ordering or endpoints, instead of a number the constants can move under.

evidence: A verbatim re-raise of F2 two rounds after the agent declined it, on an unchanged README line - the reviewer is stateless across commits, as the agent reply notes. Same verdict as F2: the em-dash convention is table-wide and verified, the conclusion is right, and the one-source-of-truth citation is pasted onto what is really a scope-and-consistency argument.

narrative: Five rounds and ten findings, and not one of the nine post-round-0 findings was caused by a fix - I checked each flagged commit and every one of them touched a different file from the line the next round flagged. The whole cost of rounds one through four was the reviewer discovering original-PR code it had already read, plus one verbatim re-raise of a finding it had been told no about. The four agent declines were each grounded in a checkable fact and all four hold. The single real bug in the PR, the skip message blaming the gradient for a MAX_REVIEW_ROUNDS cap, was found in round 3 and fixed correctly.
guidance_observations: The reviewer re-raised a declined finding verbatim two rounds later, F2 becoming F10, because each round is stateless across commits, so every no-change decline is re-litigated on every subsequent push - a direct, repeatable round cost.
Every round after the first found only original-PR code, so the marginal round did not check the fix; it re-rolled the dice on the same diff with a different scope decomposition.
One fixed-in reply posted an unexpanded git rev-parse shell substitution, leaving the thread with no usable sha.
